Neonates of the viperine water snake (Natrix maura) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that is strongly temperature-dependent. When eggs are incubated at a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the time between oviposition and the hatching event is approximately 44.2 days [ab = approximately 44.2 days]. This embryonic development duration is comparable to that reported for other European natricine species under similar thermal regimes. At the moment of egg hatching, the young-of-year reptiles measure about 13.25 cm [Lb = about 13.25 cm] in snout-vent length. Their body mass at this stage is quite modest, with wet weight at birth averaging 2.55 grams [Wwb = 2.55 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to the lecithotrophic embryo during its development within the cleidoic egg. This initial mass is a critical starting point for the juvenile growth phase, as hatchlings must begin exogenous feeding shortly after emergence to fuel their subsequent development.

The juvenile growth trajectory of Natrix maura is characterized by a steady increase in both length and mass until the individual reaches sexual maturation, though this process is markedly influenced by environmental temperature. Under conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the time since birth at puberty for males is approximately 2 years [tp = approximately 2 years], which corresponds to roughly 730 days of post-hatching life. Females, growing more slowly, typically require about 5 years since birth [tp = about 5 years since birth] to achieve gonadal activation under the same thermal conditions. This pronounced sexual bimaturism is a notable life-history feature of the species and likely relates to the differential energetic investments required for gamete production. The total length at puberty for males, a key morphological indicator of reproductive activation, is around 20.5 cm [Lp = around 20.5 cm], whereas females reach puberty, as evidenced by the first enlargement of ovarian follicles, at a larger total length of approximately 26 cm [Lp = approximately 26 cm].

Adult body size in the viperine water snake shows a pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining substantially greater dimensions than males. The maximum recorded total length for females is 85 cm, composed of a snout-vent length of 68 cm [Li = 68 cm] and a tail length of 17 cm. For males, the ultimate total length is considerably smaller, reaching approximately 40 cm [Li = approximately 40 cm] from snout to tail tip. This difference in ultimate size is accompanied by a striking disparity in adult body mass: the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown female can reach 384 grams [Wwi = 384 grams], whereas males are rarely recorded above 150 grams under similar field conditions. This substantial investment in somatic growth by females is an adaptation that supports the production of large clutches of yolk-laden eggs, as gravid female reptiles must carry the full mass of the developing clutch prior to oviposition.

Reproductive output in Natrix maura is tied to the seasonal thermal environment, and field data suggest a maximum annual reproductive rate under optimal conditions. At a sustained temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum reproductive rate, reflecting the combination of clutch size and clutch frequency, corresponds to 22 offspring per year [Ri = 22 offspring per year]. This value is derived from observations of females producing one to two clutches annually, each containing between 4 and 12 eggs. The maximum recorded longevities for this species are likewise dependent on thermal conditions; individuals maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] have a documented lifespan of approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years], making the viperine water snake one of the longer-lived European colubrids. This extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons, which is particularly advantageous for a species where females delay maturity until they have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves.

Geographic variation in life-history traits across the range of the viperine water snake likely reflects local adaptation to thermal regimes, particularly in populations inhabiting the cooler northern limit of its distribution in central France. The age at birth data, recorded under controlled incubation at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], yields the 44.2 day [ab = 44.2 day] hatching time, but wild nests exposed to fluctuating temperatures may experience eclosion that spans a broader range of 40 to 55 days. Hatchlings emerging at an average snout-vent length of 13.25 cm [Lb = 13.25 cm] and a birth mass of 2.55 grams [Wwb = 2.55 grams] face high predation pressure during their first active season. The time since birth at puberty for males, which is 2 years [tp = 2 years] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], contrasts with the five-year period required by females [tp = five-year period required by females], a difference that shapes the population's overall breeding structure and allelic diversity across successive generations.
